analysis.one_liner: Exempts licensed funeral directors and embalmers from federal minimum wage and overtime rules.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors and never advanced past its committee referral, so federal minimum wage and overtime protections for funeral directors and embalmers stayed intact.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added licensed funeral directors and licensed embalmers to the list of jobs exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal law that guarantees a minimum wage and time-and-a-half pay for hours worked beyond 40 a week. After the change, employers could have paid these workers below the minimum wage and paid nothing extra for long hours. The bill was introduced by Sen. Lindsey Graham in February 2003, sent to the Senate's labor committee, attracted no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Funeral home and funeral service employers would benefit, because they could pay licensed funeral directors and embalmers below the federal minimum wage and skip overtime pay for hours beyond 40 a week, reducing labor costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Funeral home and funeral service employers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have removed licensed funeral directors and licensed embalmers from federal minimum wage and overtime requirements under the Fair Labor Standards Act, saving affected employers those labor costs.
The change was written as a narrow amendment adding one new paragraph to the FLSA's list of exemptions, covering only employees working as licensed funeral directors or licensed embalmers.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed funeral directors and embalmers — the workers themselves — would pay, in the form of possibly sub-minimum pay and no time-and-a-half for the long, irregular hours the profession often requires.

drawbacks.text: The exemption applied only to employees holding a funeral director or embalmer license; other funeral home employees, such as apprentices without licenses, would have remained covered by federal wage rules.
Because the exemption removed both the minimum wage and the overtime guarantee, an affected employee could legally be paid below the federal minimum and receive no premium pay for long hours.

Funeral directors and embalmers commonly work long, irregular hours — evenings, weekends, and holidays are part of the job — so overtime pay is a meaningful part of compensation for many in the field, which is the cost an honest supporter of the exemption would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits and costs are almost entirely one-sided. The only gain is to employers, who would save on wages and overtime; the cost is borne by the workers themselves, a licensed trade that often works long, unpredictable hours. There is no offsetting benefit to consumers or the public identified in the record, and the bill's death left the existing wage floor untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; the Congress ended without any hearing, vote, or further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Lindsey Graham introduced the bill on February 4, 2003, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

The action history shows no activity after the February 4, 2003 referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 without the bill ever coming to a vote.
Because the bill never became law, the Fair Labor Standards Act's minimum wage and overtime requirements continued to apply to licensed funeral directors and embalmers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Funeral directors and embalmers came out ahead: their federal right to at least the minimum wage and overtime pay for long hours was never taken away, and employers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 4, 2003 to exempt licensed funeral directors and embalmers from federal minimum wage and overtime requirements.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over wage law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 4, 2003 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough to reveal a partisan split: it had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes.

industries.industry: Funeral homes and funeral service employers
industries.note: The bill would have freed employers of licensed funeral directors and embalmers from paying the federal minimum wage or time-and-a-half for overtime, lowering their labor costs. The gain comes directly out of the pay of the workers in the same establishments.
